title: What is a Living Document

sections.name: The core idea
sections.text: the core idea a living document is the default shape for anything worth a reader's attention. it is one self-contained html page, served locally, that listens. talk to the page, not a chatbot the reader selects a sentence, picks an element, or leaves a page note. the comment is the unit of conversation, anchored to the exact text it is about. the agent edits in place there is no separate reply thread. the agent changes the document itself, then the page reloads with scroll preserved and walks the reader to each change. self-contained + local one html page, served from localhost by a stdlib http server. no build pipeline, no framework, no network dependency for the core.

sections.name: When to reach for it
sections.text: when to reach for it any time a reader should be able to respond to a document instead of replying in chat. proposals and designs draft something the reader can comment on sentence-by-sentence — the open decisions sit waiting to be clicked. existing static html if you already have a folder of *.html and only want commenting, skip straight to move 3 (serve). the engine works on any folder of pages.

title: From Zero to a Listening Doc

sections.name: The one command
sections.text: the one command one script injects the widget and starts the server. setup.sh runs inject + serve, picks a free port (33333+), prints the url, and returns — the server keeps serving after it exits, for 24h past the last touch. if the server fails to come up, setup.sh says so loudly instead of printing a url that nothing answers. open the http:// url, not file:// only the served copy listens. a file:// page renders but shows no widget — the injected tags resolve /lib/* through the server.

sections.name: Then arm the watcher
sections.text: then arm the watcher without a monitor on the inbox you are collecting comments nobody reads. this is the step that closes the loop. stddoc serve — watcher built-in `stddoc serve` does two jobs in one process: it streams each new inbox entry via the monitor and writes a presence heartbeat to feedback/watcher.json so the reader's page shows a calm '● watching' dot. no separate watch script needed. don't poll in a loop let the monitor notification arrive. polling burns context for nothing.

title: Move 1

sections.name: Top-down, not wish-list
sections.text: top-down, not wish-list don't write bottom-up ('here's what we have, here's what we could add'). start with the single artifact the reader will look at, then at every layer ask: for this to exist, what must be true the layer below? the forcing function the endpoint conscripts every layer beneath it, so you never have to argue for the prerequisites — the top line visibly demands them. the proof of the proposal is the unwind itself. two honesty rules separate net-new from reuse ruthlessly (trust comes from not rebuilding what exists), and name the one unglamorous gotcha out loud as its own layer.

sections.name: The seven beats
sections.text: the seven beats the skeleton has a block for each beat. 1. the one-sentence ask concrete, human, what-they-get — not 'a system'. 2. the method box state that the endpoint is the forcing function. 3. layer 0 — render the endpoint show the actual artifact in colour; list its hard properties (each secretly names a prerequisite). 4. the descent the vertical stack, each layer joined by '↑ cannot … without'; tag every layer net-new or reuse; light the bottom green. 5. the diagrams one per load-bearing idea (six idioms — see move 2). 6. fold it forward the same chain as a build table, phase 0…n; call out reuse vs the honest first brick. 7. the calls end on the 1–3 decisions genuinely the reader's to make; mark them '◀ your call'; commit your own lean first, then invite override.

title: Move 2

sections.name: Never invent a hue
sections.text: never invent a hue paste the :root block from the skeleton verbatim. colour is meaning, not decoration. green already built · 'we stand here' · a passing test red the gap · the missing piece · the root-cause column gold the tender/relational lane · held, not actioned lavender/purple a question · a call · '◀ your call' cyan the spine · the endpoint · the primary action blue a second 'built' axis (sits beside green without clashing)

title: Move 3

sections.name: Three parts, all stdlib
sections.text: three parts, all stdlib the engine depends on nothing but go's standard library — one static binary, no install, no pip, no node. stddoc serve — inject built-in the `stddoc serve` subcommand injects the feedback link/script pair into every *.html (idempotent) and creates the feedback files on first run. re-running regenerates them if stripped. go net/http server a stdlib http server (go net/http): serves pages, accepts the comment post, exposes /info and routes /lib/* to the embedded go/stddoc-lib/lib/. feedback.js / feedback.css the browser client: floating 💬, select-to-comment, structured controls, presence, threaded history. polls history.json and auto-reloads on a new batch.

sections.name: Structured controls
sections.text: structured controls when the answer is really 'which of these?', embed a radio / checkbox / select. the reader answers by picking; the selection lands as a structured control comment with no prose to parse. pure-markup authoring a div with data-cf-control + data-cf-id + data-cf-prompt and labelled inputs. the library wires the control and a submit button and styles it from the palette. lock the choice in to reply, read the value and anchor on the control's data-cf-id (a real id in the html, unlike runtime cf_ids).

title: Move 4

sections.name: The two-part reply
sections.text: the two-part reply when the monitor fires, read the full inbox entry for the exact ids, then reply in two parts. part a — edit the html make the change they asked for and wrap the changed region in an anchor: data-cf-change='ch-<slug>'. one anchor per change. locate the spot by the quote text — anchor.cf_id is assigned at page-load and is not in your file. part b — append to history.json newest last; keep it a valid array. the batch carries comments (echoed back) and changes (id, in_response_to, anchor, title, description). in_response_to must contain the comment id — that clears the 'processing…' banner; anchor must equal a data-cf-change you actually placed.

sections.name: The etiquette
sections.text: the etiquette promptness is the soul of it. answer what's there even a test comment deserves a real in-doc reply — that is the proof the loop works. act in the document first, chat second make the change visible: a green panel, a re-coloured cell. when they answer a call, commit restyle the chosen option as decided.

title: The Pluggable Renderer

sections.name: Why it exists
sections.text: why it exists a doc engine that documents a large, evolving system must grow new visuals without a whole-system release. the renderer splits into a stable core and a swappable library of primitives, so a new component is one self-contained module against a frozen contract. the core owns the doc-tree walk, node numbering, left-nav, anchors (data-cf-change / data-cf-anchor), css/asset dedup, freeze orchestration, the palette, and the security gate. it never knows what a 'swimlane' is. the library 37 first-party primitives — 30 template-driven (data → html by a declarative template in go/stddoc-lib/templates.json) plus 7 code-driven (sections, diagrams, diagram, statetrack, swimlane, tree, evidence). each turns one typed block into html and nothing more. the moat no other doc engine binds one named-entity palette across every component and closes the agent-edits-back loop. comment capture is commodity; this pairing is not.

sections.name: How it was built — strangler-fig
sections.text: how it was built — strangler-fig the renderer was not rewritten in place. today's hand-ordered render_node was wrapped as primitives byte-identical first (the golden-master gate), then the core was hollowed out behind the contract. decisions d1–d6 build the renderer + palette (the moat); adopt only the diagram layer (d2 binary, mermaid fallback). clean-room a small registry (studied markdown-it-py, depend on none) — 85 loc in the shipped go. port the token→css pattern (style dictionary's idea), stay dependency-free. contract is language-agnostic, which is why the go port re-implemented it without re-designing — conformance 8/8 byte-identical. phased p0–p6 p0 contract + probes → p1 strangler-wrap existing renderers → p2 blocks[]+lint → p3 palette + palette-bound primitives → p4 d2 diagrams → p5 security gate → p6 standalone bespoke pages.

title: The Contract

sections.name: The contract, as the binary ships it
sections.text: the contract, as the binary ships it go/internal/registry/registry.go defines the one stable surface. a primitive is a render func plus its css, installed under a type — no class, no inheritance. the leaner-than-the-reference shape is deliberate: freeze and the palette live in the core/gate, not on every primitive, so registering one is just three things. type : string the registry key / json discriminator. the block's `type` selects exactly this handler. renderfunc(block, ctx) -> (html, error) the inner html for one block. the core wraps the anchor around your output; an error you return is caught at the boundary, never propagated. css : string css this primitive needs, registered alongside the func. collected once and deduped by the core. the boundary — register then render register(type, fn, css) installs the handler; render(type, block, ctx) dispatches it with a boundary — an unknown type or a func returning an error becomes a visible error block, never an exception that breaks the page, never a silent drop.

sections.name: The five invariants you must honor
sections.text: the five invariants you must honor from protocol/primitives.md — the rules a primitive author cannot break. 1 · anchors are core, never yours emit content only; the core assigns data-cf-anchor. never write your own data-cf-*. 2 · freeze = zero external refs freeze() output must contain no http(s)://, protocol-relative //host, or cdn src/href. the gate scans it (attributes/css + inline scripts) and fails the build naming the offending page. 3 · stdlib only no third-party dependencies — the shipped binary is one static go executable (http, json, html-escape, crypto are all stdlib; d2 renders in-process). nothing to audit in a supply chain. 4 · helpers arrive via ctx never import the core. ctx carries esc, palette, registry, anchor, render_evidence, status_class — keeping the contract language-agnostic for the go port. 5 · be palette-bound where it makes sense ctx['palette'].var(key) returns var(--ent-<key>) and raises loudly on an undeclared entity.

title: The Registry

sections.name: Three jobs
sections.text: three jobs a type→handler map plus a dispatch that can never break the page. studied markdown-it-py's renderer.rules and mjml's component registry; took the shape, wrote our own, depend on neither. register(type, fn, css) install a render func and its css under a type. has(type) reports membership; types() lists them sorted. css(type) fetch a type's static css ("" if none) — the core collects and dedupes these once per page. render(type, block, ctx) dispatch with a boundary: an unknown type or a func returning an error yields a visible error block (the sphinx rule) — never an exception that breaks the page, never a silent drop. always returns (html, nil).

title: The Palette Engine

sections.name: How it works
sections.text: how it works a doc declares one named-entity palette at root. the engine compiles it to css custom properties (--ent-<key>) and hands primitives a helper to reference an entity's color. palette.var(key) returns var(--ent-<key>). one declared set colors chips, callouts, card-grids, tables and (via d2 theme interpolation) diagrams. expand_chips(text, palette) inline entity-chip expansion in prose. paletteerror — loud on typo referencing an undeclared entity is a loud error, never a silently colorless component.

title: The blocks[] Stream + Assembled Lint

sections.name: How a node becomes blocks
sections.text: how a node becomes blocks the core walks a typed blocks[] and dispatches each through the registry. today's friendly node schema (badges / diagrams / children / sections / evidence) is mapped onto that stream by adapt_node — byte-identical to the former hand-ordered render_node. adapt_node(node) maps the friendly schema to blocks in the fixed node_block_order; author-placed body blocks slot between sections and evidence. lint ≡ renderer the lint schema is assembled from the installed primitives' validate(), so it can never drift from the renderer. an unknown block type is a lint error, mirroring the render-time error boundary.

title: The Security Gate

sections.name: Per-primitive freeze enforcement
sections.text: per-primitive freeze enforcement on --freeze every page's frozen output is scanned for external references. any leak fails the build loudly, naming the offending page. pass 1 — attribute & css scan flags src=/href= values that are absolute (https:) or root-relative (/), and css url() references to a remote https origin. the // is required, so prose that merely mentions the url(https:) form is not a leak. pass 2 — inline-script exfil scan inside <script>…</script> blocks, flags a value-shaped http(s):// url (the fetch()/.src=/location= shape) so an inline exfiltration can't slip past the attribute scan. the w3c svg namespace (www.w3.org) is excluded. scan finds, enforce names the page the two-pass scan returns the leaks; enforce raises a plain 'freeze blocked' error naming every offending page (not a typed exception).

title: D2 Diagrams + Standalone-Page Mode

sections.name: D2 helper — degrade, never fail
sections.text: d2 helper — degrade, never fail diagram primitives compile a json spec to d2 source and ask this module to render it to svg. if the d2 binary is absent we do not fail the build. have_d2() / render_svg() availability probe + render. the generated d2 source is binary-independent, so the page still carries the diagram's meaning even when d2 is missing. source_block() loud skip emits a labeled 'diagram source' block plus a loud skip note — mirroring mermaid-cli freeze behavior.

sections.name: Standalone single-page mode
sections.text: standalone single-page mode some artifacts are not doc-tree node pages but one bespoke page (e.g. the hand-authored state-machine.html). a source.json opts in with layout: page + theme + a top-level blocks[]. render_page() + load_theme() renders one page from a blocks[] stream through the registry, with a minimal bespoke shell and a named theme stylesheet (themes/<name>.css) shipped inline. anchor_attr(block) primitives read ctx['anchor_attr'](block) to stamp data-cf-change on their own root element — the std-doc anchor convention this page uses.

title: Write Your Own Plugin

sections.name: Step 1 — the minimum (render only)
sections.text: step 1 — the minimum (render only) a declarative primitive is a template entry in go/stddoc-lib/templates.json — no go code at all. a code-driven primitive is a go func registered via reg.register(type, func, css). both return content html — never an anchor (the core wraps that). pull helpers from ctx (palette, esc); never import the core. declarative (templates.json entry) add a key to go/stddoc-lib/templates.json with a template string. the engine auto-registers it — no go edit required. that is a complete, shippable primitive. author a block in a node's blocks[]:  { "type": "note", "text": "heads up." } — it renders where the block asks, nowhere else.

sections.name: Step 2 — the full seven members
sections.text: step 2 — the full seven members for a code-driven primitive (go func), here is the full contract. register three things via reg.register(); the gate and palette live in the core, not on every primitive. type : string the registry key / json discriminator. the block's `type` selects exactly this handler. required. renderfunc(block, ctx) -> (html, error) inner html for one block. required. the core wraps the anchor; you emit content only (invariant 1). an error you return is caught at the boundary — never propagated. css : string any css your component needs, passed as a string to register(). the core collects it once and dedups — pass the same string from every call and it appears in the page <style> a single time. freeze via gate zero-external rewrite for a frozen snapshot is enforced by the gate, not per-primitive. diagram primitives inline their svg via the freeze path. text primitives that emit no external refs pass automatically (invariant 2). validate (optional) return a slice of findings for a malformed block — each a {level, slug, message} (level ∈ error/warn); empty slice = valid. `stddoc lint` assembles every installed primitive's validate() into one report and publish aborts loudly on any error, so the schema can never drift from the renderer.

sections.name: Step 3 — be palette-bound
sections.text: step 3 — be palette-bound if your component shows entity colour, bind it to the one declared palette instead of hard-coding hex. this is the moat — one palette colours every component. ctx['palette'].var(key) returns var(--ent-<key>). use it in your style attribute. referencing an undeclared entity raises paletteerror loudly — a typo can never silently render colourless (invariant 5).

sections.name: Step 4 — register + test
sections.text: step 4 — register + test two lines and a test file. the golden-master guarantees you broke nothing. register (templates.json or install.go) for a declarative primitive: add a key to go/stddoc-lib/templates.json — the engine picks it up automatically (no go edit). for a code-driven primitive: call reg.register(type, fn, css) in go/internal/core/install.go. that is the only place the core learns your type exists. add a go test one test per primitive is the convention — pin renderfunc output and validate rules. run `cd go && go test ./...`. golden-master keeps the peace go/internal/core/conformance_test.go holds reference html; the strangler proof diffs every existing page byte-for-byte, so a new primitive can never silently change pages that don't use it.

title: Move 0

sections.name: Why it's called Move 0
sections.text: why it's called move 0 std-doc is four moves: method, style, serve, respond. this is not a fifth — it's a move 0: an optional pre-step that runs in front of move 1, and only when a document is structured (many pages over one knowledge base). a single hand-authored page skips it entirely and the four moves are unchanged. it's numbered 0, not 5, precisely because it's additive and comes first — count it if you like, but the method is still four moves.

sections.name: Why a doc-tree
sections.text: why a doc-tree when a document is structured — many pages over one knowledge base — author a canonical source.json and let the html be 100% derived. a publisher that renders a complete page from json alone proves the json had everything; the html can't drift because it's regenerated, never edited. stddoc publish derives html from source.json and wires the feedback widget every run (so it can't be stripped by a rewrite). the go binary at go/cmd/stddoc handles this in the `publish` subcommand. stddoc serve — auto-rebuild in watch mode with `stddoc serve`, saving source.json triggers an automatic rebuild of the published html — no separate watch script needed. stddoc freeze `stddoc freeze` bakes a portable, server-free snapshot. freezing mermaid diagram docs needs the mermaid cli — the binary refuses rather than ship broken diagrams. d2 diagrams render in-process and freeze cleanly.

sections.name: The schema
sections.text: the schema title + nodes[] are required; each node needs slug + title. everything else is optional. a node becomes one html page with sections → items, optional diagrams, badges, and an additive free-form evidence drill-down. additive by design the evidence object is free-form and ignored by any renderer that doesn't opt in — proven by injecting a sample on every node and diffing to a byte-identical render. multi-page note all pages share one feedback/ dir, so when you reply set the change's page field — that's what makes history click-to-navigate across pages.

title: Lifecycle

sections.name: JSON is the durable artifact
sections.text: json is the durable artifact an ad-hoc doc can live and die with the session. a doc worth keeping is versioned: roll stamps the canonical source.json into a git home — every version a room you can walk back into. the served html is derived and ephemeral; the json is what endures. roll — version into a home roll stamps the canonical source.json into a git home (the archive/palace). because json is canon and html is derived, the json is the artifact worth keeping; you can always re-publish the page from it. every roll is a room you can walk back into. graduate — shed a comment round graduate closes the current feedback round and keeps the doc live for the next one. the conversation moves forward without losing the page — a document is a room; the palace is the archive.

title: Gotchas

sections.name: Serving
sections.text: serving the server is tiny and stdlib-only — which means a few sharp edges. a doc's life is measured in touches, not in shells serve stays up for 24 hours after the last touch — a page load or an edit to the served files. an open tab polls, so a reader keeps it alive for free; so does an author editing with no tab open. --idle-timeout n sets a different window; --idle-timeout 0 means never exit. the server outlives the thing that started it — on purpose it used to run a parent-death watchdog by default, so setup.sh, `nohup … &`, and an agent's run_in_background all killed the doc ~5s after launching it, usually before the reader had clicked the link. parentage says nothing about whether anyone wants the document. if you do want a doc that dies with the session that made it, ask for it: --exit-with-parent. macos has no setsid — and you no longer need it a plain `&` or run_in_background is enough, now that the server doesn't kill itself when it is orphaned. don't reach for setsid; it isn't there.

sections.name: Authoring & files
sections.text: authoring & files the traps that have actually cost time. widget tags wiped by full html rewrites the widget tags live in the html, so regenerating a page from scratch silently strips them. re-run `stddoc serve` (which injects) or `stddoc publish` (which re-wires automatically) after any hand-rewrite. history.json is append-only append, never prepend or overwrite — the client walks from the end to find the latest batch. mermaid dark-theme traps three silent bombs: emoji in subgraph labels, \n in pipe edge labels, bootstrap classdef colors on a dark theme. see protocol/mermaid-gotchas.md for fixes and confirm zero bomb icons in a browser.

title: The Test Suite

sections.name: What's covered
sections.text: what's covered go/internal/ carries go test suites — one per major package plus the byte-identical conformance gate that makes the architecture trustworthy. per-package tests go/internal/registry, go/internal/palette, go/internal/gate, go/internal/template — each package's render + validate behaviour is pinned. cross-cutting guarantees registry (dispatch + error boundary), palette (var + paletteerror), gate (freeze leak fails loud), template (declarative primitive rendering), conformance (byte-identical page output). golden-master conformance gate go/internal/core/conformance_test.go holds reference html; the strangler proof diffs new renders against them to guarantee existing pages stay byte-identical when primitives are added.
